strong.text: You came through the breast cancer journey with no objective showing a gap. Where you hesitated, you recovered. Keep the review cards on a 1, 3, 7 day schedule so the outdated PYQ keys (cervix, FNAC, Halsted, M1) stay replaced under exam pressure.

mixed.text: You hold part of this topic firmly and part is still loose. The pattern in breast cancer is that many exam keys changed (core biopsy, N3c, MRM or BCS), so a loose area usually means an old key is still active. Start with the objectives marked below, then the review cards.

weak.text: Several objectives show gaps, which is common here: breast cancer has many outdated PYQ keys and look-alike staging categories. Your path shows where the old answers are still in charge. Take the objectives below one at a time, beginning with the ones you answered while sure.

secure.text: Most-common questions are secure: breast is the commonest female cancer, upper outer quadrant the commonest site, NST the commonest type, and cervix was only the older key.

shaky.text: Most-common answers are partly secure. Fix the three anchors: breast cancer now leads in India, upper outer quadrant is the commonest site, invasive ductal NST is the commonest type. Redo the O1 card.

gap.text: Most-common answers are a gap. Breast has overtaken cervix as the commonest cancer in Indian women, and the PYQs that expected cervix are older. Pair each superlative with its answer on the O1 card before the next attempt.

secure.text: Lobular versus ductal and the BRCA pairs are secure: single-file cells with E-cadherin loss mean lobular, BRCA1 sits on 17q and BRCA2 on 13q with male breast cancer.

shaky.text: Lobular versus ductal or the BRCA pairs are partly secure. Keep the two sets apart: lobular means single file, bilateral, odd metastatic sites; BRCA2 means 13q and male breast cancer. Redo the O2 card.

gap.text: Lobular versus ductal and the BRCA pairs are a gap. Ductal is commonest, but lobular is the type that is single file, multicentric and spreads to peritoneum and ovary. BRCA1 is 17q, BRCA2 is 13q and male cancer. Rebuild both pairs from the O2 card.

secure.text: Work-up choices are secure: core needle biopsy over FNAC because it shows invasion and ER, PR and HER2, ultrasound under 35, mammography after about 35 to 40.

shaky.text: Work-up choices are partly secure. Say the reason aloud: core biopsy gives histology and receptors, FNAC is kept for nodes and cysts, and age picks ultrasound or mammography. Redo the O3 card.

gap.text: Work-up choices are a gap. The older PYQ key was FNAC, but current practice is core biopsy because only it gives invasion and receptor status, and age decides ultrasound versus mammography. Revise the O3 card, then the triple assessment.

secure.text: Staging scans and prognosis are secure: routine imaging is for locally advanced or symptomatic disease, bone is the commonest metastatic site, and axillary node status is the top prognostic factor.

shaky.text: Staging scans are partly secure. Tie the scan to stage and symptoms, not to where metastases usually go. Bone is common, node status is the main prognostic factor. Redo the O4 card.

gap.text: Staging scans are a gap. Bone being the commonest metastatic site does not mean every patient is scanned; early asymptomatic disease skips routine imaging, while locally advanced or symptomatic disease gets it. Revise the O4 card.

secure.text: T category is secure: peau d'orange alone is T4b, T4d needs the red, warm inflammatory picture, and pectoralis major alone is not chest wall.

shaky.text: T category is partly secure. Keep the T4 set apart: ribs, intercostals and serratus are T4a, skin signs are T4b, T4d needs the inflammatory picture. Redo the O5 card.

gap.text: T category is a gap. A sign is not a syndrome: peau d'orange alone is T4b, T4d needs the red, warm picture over one-third of the breast, and pectoralis major alone is not T4a. Rebuild the T4 ladder from the O5 card.

secure.text: N and M are secure: ipsilateral supraclavicular nodes are N3c, and you place nodes on the ladder by position.

shaky.text: N and M are partly secure. Rehearse the ladder by position: axilla N1 or N2a, internal mammary N2b, infraclavicular N3a, supraclavicular N3c. Redo the O6 card.

gap.text: N and M are a gap. Older keys called supraclavicular nodes M1, but current AJCC staging says N3c. Walk the N ladder by anatomical position on the O6 card until each rung has its place.

secure.text: Operation choice is secure: current practice is BCS with radiotherapy or MRM, and Halsted is the one that removes both pectoral muscles.

shaky.text: Operation choice is partly secure. Hold the contrast: MRM spares pectoralis major, Halsted removes it and pectoralis minor, and BCS plus radiotherapy matches mastectomy for survival in suitable cases. Redo the O7 card.

gap.text: Operation choice is a gap. Older keys gave Halsted, but bigger is not better: BCS with radiotherapy gives equivalent survival, and MRM spares pectoralis major. Review the O7 card on what each operation removes.

secure.text: Surgical decisions are secure: you separate BCS contraindications from size alone, stage a clinically node-negative axilla with SLNB, and give radiotherapy after BCS.

shaky.text: Surgical decisions are partly secure. Build the BCS contraindications from logic (multicentric, prior radiotherapy, pregnancy, persistent positive margins) and keep SLNB for cN0 and ALND for node-positive. Redo the O8 card.

gap.text: Surgical decisions are a gap. Size alone does not forbid BCS, and the axilla is staged by SLNB before it is dissected when nodes are clinically negative. Rebuild both lists from the O8 card.

secure.text: Treatment sequence is secure: locally advanced and inflammatory cancers get neoadjuvant chemotherapy before surgery, with radiotherapy after.

shaky.text: Treatment sequence is partly secure. Rehearse the order with its reason: chemotherapy first to downstage and treat spread, then MRM, then radiotherapy. Redo the O9 card.

gap.text: Treatment sequence is a gap. The operation does not go first in locally advanced or inflammatory disease; chemotherapy comes first to treat spread and shrink the tumour. Rehearse chemotherapy, MRM, radiotherapy on the O9 card.

secure.text: Hormonal therapy is secure: you read menopausal status to pick tamoxifen or an aromatase inhibitor, and you know tamoxifen raises endometrial cancer risk and classic LCIS is watched.

shaky.text: Hormonal therapy is partly secure. Re-read the qualifier each time: premenopausal means tamoxifen, postmenopausal means aromatase inhibitor, and tamoxifen carries endometrial risk. Redo the O10 card.

gap.text: Hormonal therapy is a gap. ER-positive is not enough: menopausal status decides the drug, tamoxifen is a partial agonist in the endometrium, and classic LCIS is a risk marker, not a mastectomy indication. Revise the O10 card.

secure.text: The HER2 drug is secure: trastuzumab has usually reversible, non-dose-related cardiotoxicity, unlike doxorubicin.

shaky.text: The HER2 drug is partly secure. Keep the pair apart: trastuzumab is reversible and not dose-related, doxorubicin is cumulative and largely irreversible. Redo the O11 card.

gap.text: The HER2 drug is a gap. Trastuzumab and doxorubicin are both cardiotoxic, but trastuzumab is usually reversible and not dose-related. Compare them side by side on the O11 card.

secure.text: Axillary dissection complications are secure: intercostobrachial injury gives medial arm numbness and is commonest, long thoracic injury gives winging.

shaky.text: Axillary dissection complications are partly secure. Pair each nerve to its deficit, then separate frequency from drama: intercostobrachial is commonest, long thoracic is the dramatic one. Redo the O12 card.

gap.text: Axillary dissection complications are a gap. Winging is memorable, but intercostobrachial injury is the commonest, with numbness of the medial upper arm. Pair each nerve to its deficit on the O12 card.

avoided.text: Core biopsy over FNAC: you kept the current key.

fell_recovered.text: You moved from the old FNAC key to core biopsy. It can return under pressure, so ask each time what the pathologist must report.

fell_open.text: You treated FNAC as the breast test, the old PYQ key. You may have corrected on the spot, but meet it again on a fresh question. Core biopsy shows invasion and ER, PR and HER2; FNAC suits nodes and cysts. Revisit the O3 review card.

avoided.text: Supraclavicular nodes as N3c: you held the current key.

fell_recovered.text: You replaced the old M1 key with N3c. Under pressure the old key can return, so place the node on the ladder by position first.

fell_open.text: You filed supraclavicular nodes as distant disease, the older key. You may have corrected on the spot, but meet it again on a fresh question. Current AJCC says N3c. Revisit the O6 review card and walk the N ladder.

avoided.text: Halsted versus current surgery: you knew it has de-escalated.

fell_recovered.text: You updated from Halsted to BCS plus radiotherapy or MRM. The urge to pick the biggest operation can return, so ask what survival data support.

fell_open.text: You treated 'radical' as definitive, so Halsted stayed the standard. You may have corrected on the spot, but meet it again on a fresh question. Current practice is BCS with radiotherapy or MRM. Revisit the O7 review card on what Halsted removes.

avoided.text: Breast as commonest female cancer: you held the current key.

fell_recovered.text: You dropped the cervix key for breast. The remembered PYQ can come back under pressure, so check whether epidemiology has changed.

fell_open.text: You answered with the old key, cervix as the commonest cancer in Indian women. You may have corrected on the spot, but meet it again on a fresh question. Breast has overtaken cervix. Revisit the O1 review card.

avoided.text: Routine imaging: you did not over-order scans.

fell_recovered.text: You moved from scanning everyone to scanning by stage and symptoms. The bone-metastasis link can pull you back, so check stage first.

fell_open.text: You linked bone being the commonest metastatic site to a routine scan for every patient. You may have corrected on the spot, but meet it again on a fresh question. Imaging is for locally advanced or symptomatic disease. Revisit the O4 review card.

avoided.text: Trastuzumab versus doxorubicin: you kept the two apart.

fell_recovered.text: You separated trastuzumab from doxorubicin. Both are cardiotoxic, so the merge can return, so recall dose relation and reversibility each time.

fell_open.text: You carried the anthracycline pattern onto trastuzumab, as dose-dependent and irreversible. You may have corrected on the spot, but meet it again on a fresh question. Trastuzumab is usually reversible and not dose-related. Revisit the O11 review card.

avoided.text: Reading menopausal status: you did not default to tamoxifen.

fell_recovered.text: You began reading menopausal status instead of stopping at ER-positive. Exam stems may hide the status, so look for it first.

fell_open.text: You stopped at ER-positive and used tamoxifen as the default. You may have corrected on the spot, but meet it again on a fresh question. Premenopausal means tamoxifen; postmenopausal means an aromatase inhibitor. Revisit the O10 review card.

avoided.text: Lobular versus ductal: you matched the picture, not the frequency.

fell_recovered.text: You moved off the ductal default to lobular where the stem showed single-file cells. The pull of 'commonest' can return, so read the pattern.

fell_open.text: You defaulted to ductal NST because it is commonest. You may have corrected on the spot, but meet it again on a fresh question. Single file, E-cadherin loss and bilateral or multicentric disease mean lobular. Revisit the O2 review card.

avoided.text: Peau d'orange as T4b: you separated sign from syndrome.

fell_recovered.text: You stopped tying peau d'orange to T4d. The reverse error can appear in an inflammatory stem, so ask for the clinical picture.

fell_open.text: You matched peau d'orange to inflammatory carcinoma, T4d. You may have corrected on the spot, but meet it again on a fresh question. Peau d'orange alone is T4b; T4d needs the red, warm picture over one-third of the breast. Revisit the O5 review card.

avoided.text: Chest wall in T4a: your list was right.

fell_recovered.text: You removed pectoralis from the T4a list. Muscle fixity is a tempting cue, so rebuild the list from ribs, intercostals and serratus.

fell_open.text: You padded the T4a chest-wall list with pectoralis major. You may have corrected on the spot, but meet it again on a fresh question. T4a is ribs, intercostals and serratus anterior. Revisit the O5 review card.

avoided.text: BCS contraindications: you built the list from logic.

fell_recovered.text: You dropped size alone from the contraindications. Size relative to the breast, and downstaging, can mislead again, so ask whether margins and radiotherapy are possible.

fell_open.text: You treated a tumour over 5 cm as an absolute bar to BCS, carrying the staging size into the surgical list. You may have corrected on the spot, but meet it again on a fresh question. Revisit the O8 review card on BCS contraindications.

avoided.text: Nerve injured most often: you separated common from dramatic.

fell_recovered.text: You separated the commonest nerve injury from the most dramatic one. Winging is vivid and can return, so pair each nerve to its deficit.

fell_open.text: You linked winging of the scapula to the nerve most often injured, so you picked long thoracic. You may have corrected on the spot, but meet it again on a fresh question. Intercostobrachial is commonest. Revisit the O12 review card.

avoided.text: Treatment sequence: you put chemotherapy first when needed.

fell_recovered.text: You moved the operation behind neoadjuvant chemotherapy in advanced disease. Surgery feels decisive and can return under pressure, so ask what must come first.

fell_open.text: You named the right treatments but put the operation first in advanced or inflammatory cancer. You may have corrected on the spot, but meet it again on a fresh question. Order is chemotherapy, MRM, radiotherapy. Revisit the O9 review card.

avoided.text: Bloody discharge: you kept 'most common' separate from 'most worrying'.

fell_recovered.text: You separated 'most common cause' from 'cause to exclude'. The alarm of bloody discharge can pull you back to carcinoma, so keep the qualifier.

fell_open.text: You read 'most common' as 'most worrying' and answered carcinoma for bloody nipple discharge. You may have corrected on the spot, but meet it again on a fresh question. The commonest cause is intraductal papilloma. Revisit the O5 review card.

avoided.text: Axillary order: you staged before dissecting.

fell_recovered.text: You fixed the order to SLNB in clinically node-negative disease. The old dissect-first habit can return, so ask what the axilla needs.

fell_open.text: You kept the old order, with axillary dissection first. You may have corrected on the spot, but meet it again on a fresh question. Clinically node-negative disease gets SLNB; biopsy-proven node-positive disease goes to ALND. Revisit the O8 review card.

avoided.text: BRCA chromosomes: your numbers were anchored.

fell_recovered.text: You re-anchored the BRCA numbers. Number pairs fade quickly, so rehearse them again before the exam.

fell_open.text: You swapped the chromosome numbers, 13q for BRCA1 and 17q for BRCA2. You may have corrected on the spot, but meet it again on a fresh question. BRCA1 is 17q, BRCA2 is 13q. Revisit the O2 review card.

avoided.text: BRCA gene and phenotype: your pairs were secure.

fell_recovered.text: You fixed the gene and phenotype pairs. BRCA1 is the famous one and can return as the default, so read which phenotype the stem describes.

fell_open.text: You attached BRCA1, the better-known gene, to male breast cancer. You may have corrected on the spot, but meet it again on a fresh question. BRCA2 goes with male cancer; BRCA1 goes with triple-negative tumours. Revisit the O2 review card.

avoided.text: Imaging by age: you checked age first.

fell_recovered.text: You began checking age before choosing imaging. The screening test can slip back in, so ask age and breast density first.

fell_open.text: You carried mammography into every age group, including women under 35. You may have corrected on the spot, but meet it again on a fresh question. Ultrasound is preferred under 35. Revisit the O3 review card.

avoided.text: Tamoxifen and the endometrium: you held the tissue-specific effect.

fell_recovered.text: You corrected the reversed mechanism. Tamoxifen blocks the breast but acts partly as an agonist in the uterus, so predict each tissue separately.

fell_open.text: You treated tamoxifen as an oestrogen blocker in every tissue, so it seemed to protect the endometrium. You may have corrected on the spot, but meet it again on a fresh question. Tamoxifen raises endometrial cancer risk; raloxifene does not. Revisit the O10 review card.

avoided.text: Classic LCIS: you treated it as a risk marker.

fell_recovered.text: You changed from operating on classic LCIS to surveillance. 'Carcinoma in situ' can still tempt you, so ask what the lesion predicts.

fell_open.text: You applied invasive-cancer treatment to classic LCIS, reading it as a cancer to remove. You may have corrected on the spot, but meet it again on a fresh question. Classic LCIS is a risk marker managed by surveillance. Revisit the O10 review card.

E1.text: You tend to merge look-alikes and match on one sign, such as peau d'orange or the commonest histology. Before answering, name the one feature that separates the pair, then check the stem has it.

E2.text: You tend to add familiar items to fixed lists, such as pectoralis in T4a or size in BCS contraindications. Rebuild each list from its logic, not from what looks related.

E3.text: You tend to reverse a mechanism, assuming a drug acts the same in every tissue. Predict the effect tissue by tissue before choosing, as with tamoxifen in breast and endometrium.

E4.text: You tend to stretch 'most common' to 'most worrying' or 'always'. Read the exact qualifier in the stem, then ask what the counter-case would be.

E5.text: You tend to answer with an older PYQ key (cervix, FNAC, Halsted, M1). Ask whether practice or staging has changed, and keep both answers ready: what PYQs expected and what current practice says.

E6.text: You tend to swap paired numbers such as 13q and 17q. Anchor each number to its gene with a hook and rehearse in both directions.

E7.text: You tend to stop reading at the diagnosis and miss the qualifier, such as menopausal status, age or setting. Underline the qualifier in the stem before choosing a drug or test.

E8.text: You tend to pick a test because of where disease usually goes, not by who needs it. Ask stage and symptoms before choosing any scan.

E9.text: You tend to name the right steps in the wrong order, with surgery or dissection first. Ask what comes first and why before sequencing.

E10.text: You tend to link a gene or nerve to its most famous association rather than the one the stem describes. Pair each with its phenotype or deficit and separate common from dramatic.

overconfident.text: You tapped Sure on at least two answers that were wrong. High-confidence errors are the best-remembered once fixed, so review those cards first and pause for one beat before tapping Sure on staging or surgery questions.

underconfident.text: You were right on several answers where you tapped Guessing. Your knowledge is ahead of your confidence, so trust the reasoning you used and tap Sure when you can state the reason.

calibrated.text: Your Sure taps matched your answers. That is useful, because you can tell what you know from what you do not. Spend revision time on the Guessing items.

hints_heavy.text: You asked for hints or explanations often. That is a sound way to learn new material, but the exam gives none. Redo the review cards without opening a hint, starting with the objectives marked shaky.

hints_none.text: You took no hints, so each trap you met was a real miss. Use the review cards on those objectives now, before the answer fades.

hinted_only.text: You reached some objectives right only after a hint. Retry those review cards cold, without help, to show you can answer unaided.

fast_lane.text: You took a skip: at least one of 'I know this, skip ahead' after the lobular and ductal question, or 'skip the worked case' on the neoadjuvant sequence. A skip saves time but not the lesson. Do the O2 and O9 review cards to check what the skipped step covered.

gap.text: Start with the cards for objectives marked gap, beginning with any trap you fell into while sure. Do one card per day on a 1, 3, 7 day schedule, then replay the segment for the weakest objective.

clear.text: No gaps showed on your path. Keep the review cards on the 1, 3, 7, 21, 60 day schedule, and test the outdated keys (cervix, FNAC, Halsted, M1) on fresh questions.
